Contract Law.description: A contract requires a definite offer by one party and an unqualified acceptance of its exact terms by the other, communicated between the parties.
Each party to a contract must give something of legal value in exchange for the other's promise; a gratuitous promise is generally unenforceable.
Displays, advertisements, and price listings are ordinarily treated as invitations for the other party to make an offer, not as offers themselves.
A contract may be voidable where one party knew, or a reasonable person ought to have known, that the other party's terms resulted from an obvious clerical or pricing error.
Both parties must share a genuine meeting of the minds on the essential terms of the agreement for a binding contract to form.
A contract may be discharged where an unforeseen event, without fault of either party, renders performance impossible or radically different from what was agreed.

Criminal Law.description: Criminal liability generally requires both a wrongful physical act (actus reus) and a culpable mental state (mens rea) occurring together.
An honest and reasonable mistaken belief about a factual circumstance can negate the specific intent required for certain offenses.
Burglary typically requires an unlawful entry accompanied by a contemporaneous intent to commit a felony or theft inside the premises.
A genuine belief that property belongs to oneself can negate the intent to permanently deprive another of it, defeating a theft charge.

Tort / Negligence.description: A defendant owes a duty of care to any person who is a reasonably foreseeable victim of the defendant's conduct.
Breach occurs when a defendant's conduct falls below what a reasonably prudent person would have done in the same circumstances.
A plaintiff must show the defendant's breach was both the factual cause and the legally proximate cause of the harm suffered.
An actor confronting a sudden, unforeseen peril not of their own making is judged against what a reasonable person would do under that emergency pressure.
An unforeseeable third-party act occurring after the defendant's conduct may break the chain of proximate causation.

Constitutional Law.description: Government action that burdens a fundamental right or uses a suspect classification must serve a compelling interest through the least restrictive means.
Government restrictions on speech that target a particular viewpoint, rather than a neutral subject matter or manner, are presumptively unconstitutional.
A law that restricts substantially more protected conduct than necessary to achieve its legitimate purpose may be struck down as overbroad.
Constitutional protections against government overreach generally apply only where the challenged conduct is attributable to the state.

Intellectual Property.description: Copyright protection attaches to original works of authorship fixed in a tangible medium, but not to facts or ideas themselves.
Limited use of copyrighted material may be permitted for purposes such as criticism, commentary, or education, weighed against factors like purpose and market effect.
Trademark infringement generally turns on whether an ordinary consumer would likely be confused about the source of competing goods or services.
Patentable inventions must be new and would not have been obvious to a person skilled in the relevant field at the time of filing.

Cyber Law.description: Accessing a computer system or network without permission, or exceeding authorized access, generally constitutes a legal violation regardless of intent to cause harm.
Processing personal data generally requires a lawful basis such as informed consent, and data must be used consistently with the purpose disclosed.
Online platforms may receive limited liability protection for third-party content if they act as neutral intermediaries and respond to takedown notices.

International Law.description: Agreements between states must be performed in good faith; a state cannot invoke its own domestic law to justify failing to perform a treaty obligation.
Each state has exclusive authority over matters within its own territory, subject to obligations it has voluntarily accepted under international law.
A practice becomes binding customary international law where there is consistent state practice combined with a belief that the practice is legally required.
